extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, and practitioners of comedy/dramatic theory (playwrights, humor theorists, literary critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic rules and principles for recognizing and producing comic effects in persons, situations, words and stagecraft, drawn from a philosophical/theoretical treatment of laughter and comedy. Emphasises mechanisms (mechanisation, repetition, suggestion, puppet-like behaviour) and theatrical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical intrudes where moral is expected
rubrics_metrics.description: Any incident is comic that calls our attention to the physical in a person, when it is the moral side that is concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and guidance: a public speaker sneezing at a pathetic moment; the phrase 'He was virtuous and plump' — the sudden recall from soul to body creates the comic. Bashfulness can seem ridiculous because it suggests a person embarrassed by his body. The tragic poet avoids bodily actions (eating, sitting) because attention to the body risks turning tragedy into comedy (Napoleon anecdote about making someone sit to cut short a tragic scene).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner substituted for matter (form overtakes spirit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy arises when manner seeks to outdo matter; when the letter aims at ousting the spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional automatism — professions where outward form and formalities are scrupulously respected regardless of ends — is laughable (examples: lawyers, magistrates, doctors speaking as if health/justice matter less than mere existence of their offices). Stage examples and quotations (Doctor Diafoirus, Doctor Bahis, Tomes, Brid’oison) show the mechanical application of rules producing ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person perceived as thing
rubrics_metrics.description: We laugh every time a person gives us the impression of being a thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: Sancho Panza tossed like a football; Baron Munchausen as a cannonball; clown routines where performers' individuality fades into inanimate objects (rubber balls, wooden dummies). Techniques producing this effect include making movements/attitudes that gradually turn flesh-and-blood into motionless or repetitive things, and using rhythm and lexical piling to suggest doll-like or animal imagery (examples from Rdgénard and Figaro).

rubrics_metrics.name: Illusion of life plus impression of mechanical arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: Any arrangement of acts and events is comic which gives us, in a single combination, the illusion of life and the distinct impression of a mechanical arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start from children's puppet games: strings and mechanical motions reappear in adult comedy. On stage, characters may be made to seem both 'alive' and 'mechanically arranged' (puppet-like), producing the comic. Theatrical simplification and magnification of life help expose those mechanical threads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition (the spring / Jack‑in‑the‑box) as core comic mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition (the bent-and-released spring image) is a central comic device: a stubborn force is repeatedly repressed and released.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical model: Punch and Judy policeman repeatedly felled and springing up. Moral/linguistic analogue: a feeling or expression that bursts forth, is checked, and springs forth again. Molière examples: Dorine/Orgon ('Et Tartuffe?'), Scapin/Géronte (avarice springing back), Harpagon ('No dowry wanted!'). The author formulates the rule: in comic repetition of words we generally find two terms — a repressed feeling which goes off like a spring; and an idea that delights in repressing the feeling anew.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puppet/Jack‑in‑the‑box imagery for staging and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Jack-in-the-box (push/pull, spring/rebound) image to create tempo and visible mechanical rhythm in scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage technique: characters entering/exiting and being 'pushed back' into wings in regular beats (Sganarelle/Pancrace example), windows opening like a lid, heads appearing as if bursting a box. The regular recurrence marks the tempo and augments the comic as spectators perceive a machine-like repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplication of ridicule by adding a physical defect overtone
rubrics_metrics.description: When a professional or moral ridiculousness (the primary comic note) is struck, comic fancy instinctively adds physical peculiarity as an overtone to complete the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Brid’oison the stammering judge whose stammer prepares us to see his intellectual ossification; Molière's doctors — one scans syllables slowly, another stutters — the rhythm/peculiarity of speech ordinarily completes professional ridicule. Actors often invent such physical defects when the author omits them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner double-personality / mechanical oscillation
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy can arise from a single character embodying two opposing, inelastic elements that oscillate mechanically (inner duel), rather than integrating into a complex living whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Alceste repeating 'I don't say that!' — the comic scene is really between Alceste and himself: one part wants brutal frankness, the other cannot deliver it. Each repetition reveals increasing internal tension until the spring goes off. Distinguish this from genuine complex character where opposing feelings coexist and produce seriousness rather than laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual suggestion: moving from vague to distinct to induce the comic image
rubrics_metrics.description: The gradual passing from the dim and vague to the clear and distinct (a method of suggestion) is effective in producing comic hallucinations of persons becoming things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to hypnotic suggestion: start from concrete perceptions and progressively make them indefinite until a new object is perceived. In poetry and prose, rhythm, rhyme and assonance can lull imagination (see RDgnard lines and Figaro example) and prepare readers to accept a fleeting image (doll/animal/thing). Use graduated hints to induce the audience to supply the comic vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy as continuation of childish games / puppet-logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is fundamentally a game that imitates life; many adult comic combinations are continuations of games played in childhood (puppets, strings, springs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dramaturgical implication: construct characters and situations by tracing how a child's play (Jack-in-the-box, puppet-strings, cat-and-mouse play) would scale up to adult social interactions. Many comic situations are formed by applying those simple mechanical contrivances to complex human relations on stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace continuity of analogies / avoid losing the original comic thread
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic forms often derive their effect by resemblance chaining: one comic image evokes another, which evokes a third, and so on; analysis and construction must hold the thread along which the comic impression travels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution for theorists/playwrights: do not lose sight of the original cause of laughter when extending analogies; the progressive continuity (the 'overtones' branching outward) is driven by a kind of living energy of comic fancy, but the chain must be coherent for the effect to be intelligible and effective.
